outcome: Study all nine media forms and study at least one audio-visual, one print and one online or social form in depth.
Use the set close study products as vehicles for the four areas of the theoretical framework.
Analyse and compare media products in their social, cultural, historical and political contexts.
Build a sustained, coherent, substantiated line of reasoning and draw together knowledge from across the course.
Apply semiotic analysis, including denotation and connotation, and terms such as sign, icon, symbol and anchorage.
Explain how forms of media language communicate meaning, using the sender-message-receiver model.
Explain how selection, combination and exclusion of elements shape meaning, point of view and the constructed nature of reality.
Describe register and direct and indirect modes of address.
Explain narrative theories including Propp's character types.
Describe narrative development (exposition, disruption, complication, climax, resolution) and audience appeal through enigma and closure.
Explain how technology change affects the form, content and meaning of media, such as CGI, high definition, image manipulation and user-generated content.
Analyse technical codes: shot types, camera movement, composition, lighting, editing and diegetic and non-diegetic sound.
Analyse print codes: colour, layout, typography, house style, juxtaposition and superimposition.
Analyse mise-en-scène: costume, lighting, location, actors, make-up, props and set dressing.
Analyse verbal and non-verbal codes, such as language choice, dress, body movement and paralanguage.
Explain genre theory: repetition and variation, the dynamic nature of genre and hybridity.
Explain intertextuality and what shapes genre products: finance, culture and audience demand.
Explain that media re-present the world through selection, construction and mediation, and discuss realism and 'window on the world' views.
Apply theories of gender and representation, including feminist approaches and essentialist versus social constructionist views.
Explain producers' choices in representing events and groups, including audience positioning and selective or biased representation.
Explain how reality is represented differently for different purposes, including persuasion, advertising and propaganda.
Explain how stereotypes become established, change over time, can be positive or negative, and help audiences read media quickly.
Explain how and why groups are under-represented or misrepresented, and the link to dominant societal values.
Explain how representations and self-representations convey viewpoints and values, and contrast dominant and contested representations.
Explain the social, cultural and political significance of representations, including agenda setting and news values.
Explain how representations reflect the contexts and changing values in which they were made.
Explain how age, class, gender, ethnicity and experience affect how audiences decode representations.
Explain production by large organisations and by individuals, and patterns of ownership: mergers, demergers, takeovers, concentration.
Explain how production processes, personnel, technologies, and where and when products are made affect the final product.
Explain the effects of conglomerate ownership, diversification, and vertical and horizontal integration.
Explain convergence across platforms and national settings, including cross-media ownership.
Compare government-funded, not-for-profit and commercial models, including licence fee, advertising, sponsorship and product placement.
Explain how media operate globally, including globalisation, cultural imperialism and international trade and regulation.
Explain types of regulation, and the roles of OFCOM, IPSO, VSC, BBFC, ASA and PEGI.
Discuss disputes over freedom, censorship and control.
Discuss challenges digital technologies pose for regulation: online abuse, anonymity, ISP responsibilities and public interest versus individual rights.
Explain active and passive audiences, response, interpretation, and Blumler and Katz's Uses and Gratifications theory.
Explain why products target specialised or mass audiences, and why producers create audiences to sell to advertisers.
Explain how organisations target audiences through genre conventions and marketing such as viral marketing, trailers and teasers.
Explain how audiences are segmented by geographic, demographic and psychographic variables.
Explain how technologies reach and identify audiences, and describe audience research bodies (BARB, RAJAR, Nielsen) and research methods.
Explain reception theories, preferred and aberrant readings, and how social variables lead to different interpretations over time.
Explain how media practices connect to identity, including fans, fandom and talking about the media.
Explain the themes, needs and desires, and social functions that media products address.
Explain how audience responses to historical products change as cultural values shift.
